title: Can you structure these 14 operations case questions in two minutes each?
description: 14 operations case prompts to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: Yes: follow the work from start to finish, find where it gets stuck, and structure around that bottleneck rather than around generic ideas like "more staff" or "new technology". Operations prompts reward candidates who locate the problem before fixing it. Here are 14, from emergency departments to Christmas parcels: two minutes each, then open the model and compare.
body:
How to use this set

Give yourself two minutes per prompt. Most operations structures take one of two shapes: demand versus capacity (how much work arrives, how much we can process) or the steps of the process in order (where in the chain does it go wrong?). Pick the shape, fill it with this client's specifics, and say where you would start. Then open the model. For the method in full, read how to structure a process case.

1. A hospital's emergency waiting times have doubled in a year.

Show a model structure
  • Demand: arrivals by hour and day; case mix, since older, sicker patients take longer.
  • Capacity: doctors and nurses on shift versus arrivals; cubicles and beds.
  • Process inside the department: triage, tests, waiting for a specialist; shift handovers.
  • Flow out: waiting for a ward bed; discharge and social care delays.

Where to start: flow out. In many hospitals, admitted patients waiting for a ward bed block the emergency department.

The trap: asking for more staff without checking whether patients are stuck waiting for beds.

2. A parcel company's on-time delivery fell from 95% to 85%.

Show a model structure
  • Where in the chain: collection, sorting hub, trunk haul, last mile.
  • Volume versus capacity: parcel growth versus vans, drivers and sorting hours; daily and seasonal peaks.
  • Process and systems: route planning, scanning, missed handovers; any new system or hub.
  • External: weather, traffic, partner carriers; address and access problems.

Where to start: find the step where parcels start running late. Late parcels have tripled, from 5% to 15%.

The trap: listing causes without locating where delays begin.

3. An airline's aircraft spend 20% longer on the ground between flights than rivals'.

Show a model structure
  • Arrival: waiting for a gate, stand or tug; taxi times.
  • Servicing: cleaning, catering, fuel and bags.
  • Boarding: boarding process and cabin bags; late passengers.
  • Planning: schedule buffers and crew connections; staff at peak times.

Where to start: the critical path, the longest chain of steps that must happen one after another. It sets the turnaround time, so speeding up anything off it saves nothing.

The trap: trying to speed up every task.

4. A telecom company's customer complaints have tripled in six months.

Show a model structure
  • What about: billing, network, installation or support; which category grew.
  • Who: new versus existing customers; region, product, sales channel.
  • What changed: a new billing system, price rise or outsourcing; timing against the rise.
  • Handling: first-call resolution; time to fix and repeat complaints.

Where to start: what changed six months ago. A tripling rarely happens without a trigger.

The trap: hiring more call-centre staff before finding the cause.

5. A furniture factory's defect rate rose from 2% to 6%.

Show a model structure
  • Where defects appear: product, line, process step and shift.
  • Materials: supplier changes and wood quality; storage and humidity.
  • People: new or temporary staff and training; overtime and fatigue.
  • Machines and process: maintenance, settings and wear; new equipment or faster line speed.

Where to start: where defects appear. Narrowing to one step usually reveals the cause.

The trap: adding inspection at the end instead of fixing the cause.

6. An airport's security queues now regularly exceed 45 minutes.

Show a model structure
  • Demand: passengers per hour; flight schedule peaks.
  • Lanes open: staff rostered versus needed; absence and hiring.
  • Speed per lane: bag rescans, liquids, scanner type; passenger preparation.
  • Layout and information: space to queue and unpack; telling passengers when to arrive.

Where to start: passengers per hour against lanes open per hour. The mismatch is usually at the peaks.

The trap: buying scanners when the problem is staffing at the peak.

7. A pharmacy chain's shelves are out of stock on 8% of items.

Show a model structure
  • Which items: fast movers versus the long tail; medicines versus retail products.
  • Supply: supplier shortages and late deliveries; wholesaler fill rate.
  • Ordering: store forecasts and reorder points; data errors.
  • In store: stock in the back but not on the shelf; shelf space and restocking.

Where to start: which items. A national medicine shortage and poor store ordering need different fixes.

The trap: blaming suppliers without checking the stockroom.

8. A bank's app rating has fallen from 4.6 to 3.2 stars.

Show a model structure
  • What reviews say: login, speed, crashes, missing features; when bad reviews began.
  • Which users: iPhone versus Android and device age; new versus existing customers.
  • What changed: an app release, new login security, removed features.
  • Response: fixes and release testing; replying to reviews.

Where to start: when the bad reviews began, lined up against release dates.

The trap: assuming it is a design problem without reading the complaints.

9. Should an insurer outsource its IT support?

Show a model structure
  • Cost: current cost versus vendor price; transition and contract management.
  • Quality: service levels and response times; knowledge of our systems.
  • Risk: data security and regulation; dependence on one vendor.
  • Alternatives: automate first; outsource only part.

Where to start: total cost including transition, compared at the same service level. See the outsourcing framework.

The trap: comparing salaries with the vendor's price and forgetting transition and oversight costs.

10. Should a US clothing brand move production from Asia to Mexico?

Show a model structure
  • Landed cost per item: labour, fabric, freight and duties; exchange rates.
  • Speed and flexibility: weeks from order to store; less unsold stock and fewer markdowns.
  • Capability: supplier skills, capacity and quality.
  • Risks and transition: switching cost and time; supply risk in each region.

Where to start: landed cost plus markdowns saved. In fashion, speed is worth money.

The trap: comparing factory prices only.

11. How can a traditional bank get more customers to use its app instead of branches?

Show a model structure
  • Why they don't: trust, habit, missing features; age and confidence.
  • Make it better: the tasks people still visit branches for; speed and reliability.
  • Help people switch: staff teaching in branches; rewards for first use.
  • Change defaults: paperless statements; fees for branch-only services.

Where to start: why they don't. Missing features and low confidence need different fixes.

The trap: pushing people online with fees before the app is good enough.

12. How can a call-centre business reduce staff turnover from 60% a year?

Show a model structure
  • Who leaves and when: new starters, shifts and teams; exit reasons.
  • Pay and hours: pay against local jobs; shift patterns and flexibility.
  • The job: call targets and stress; tools and training.
  • Managers and growth: team leaders' skills; promotion paths.

Where to start: who leaves and when. Check new starters first; early leavers often drive the rate.

The trap: raising pay for everyone before knowing why people leave.

13. How can a train operator get punctuality from 80% to 90%?

Show a model structure
  • Causes of delay: track, train, staff and passenger incidents; which routes and times.
  • Trains: maintenance and spare trains; faults per million miles.
  • Timetable: recovery time and platform use; knock-on delays.
  • People: crew availability; station dispatch.

Where to start: causes of delay. Fix the few that cause most lost minutes. The goal halves late trains, from 20% to 10%.

The trap: padding the timetable without fixing the causes.

14. How can a parcel company handle 50% more parcels at Christmas?

Show a model structure
  • Sorting capacity: extra shifts and temporary sites; automation.
  • Delivery capacity: temporary drivers and vans; weekend and evening rounds.
  • Shape demand: customer cut-off dates and pricing; lockers and pick-up points.
  • Planning: forecasts by customer; hiring and training early.

Where to start: shaping demand. Spreading volume is cheaper than adding capacity.

The trap: only hiring more people.

How to score your answer

Take the hospital prompt. A strong answer traces the patient from arrival through triage, tests, treatment and then admission or discharge, and asks where the queue builds. The numbers show why. If 100 patients arrive a day and the department can only complete 95, the backlog grows by five patients every day, before any variation. An extra triage nurse speeds up the front door but does nothing if the real constraint is a shortage of ward beds.

Check your structure for three things: did you find the binding constraint before suggesting fixes, did you compare options on safety or quality as well as cost, and could you adapt if the interviewer told you the bottleneck was somewhere else?
